claims.text: Structural and chemical stability is governed by formation of a stable, coherent interface between the constituent elements.
A stable, coherent interface suppresses atomic diffusion.
A stable, coherent interface suppresses elemental segregation.
Suppression of diffusion and segregation maintains alloy composition.
Suppression of diffusion and segregation maintains alloy microstructure.
The initial CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy nanoalloy has a uniform elemental distribution.
The initial CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy nanoalloy has an FCC crystal structure.
The proposed coherent interface is characterized by low lattice-parameter mismatch.
The proposed coherent interface is characterized by a high degree of atomic ordering.
Formation of the coherent interface reduces the driving force for phase separation.
After annealing, the high-entropy nanoalloy will retain its FCC structure.
After annealing, the high-entropy nanoalloy will retain a uniform distribution of constituent elements.
The annealed high-entropy nanoalloy will show at least a 20% reduction in lattice-parameter mismatch relative to pure Ni annealed under the same conditions.
The prediction is intended to apply from 900°C to 1100°C and from 5 to 20 hours of annealing.
Grain-boundary effects and impurity elements may influence nanoalloy stability and the validity of the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The intervention specifies annealing in an inert atmosphere, whereas the conditions specify a vacuum environment; these are distinct environmental controls unless a vacuum plus inert-gas protocol is explicitly defined.

The lattice-mismatch comparison is internally ill-defined: pure Ni has no constituent-to-constituent lattice mismatch, and the predicted ≥20% reduction is not expressed on the same unambiguous scale as the falsification threshold of mismatch greater than 10% relative to baseline.
